title: The golden deer and the five turnings
hookLine: a golden deer, a false cry in Rama's voice, and Patanjali's map of everything a mind does
carry: five turnings, and even true knowing is one
tomorrow: how do you hold a mind as restless as the wind?
last: THE SEER IS NOT THE THOUGHTS IT SEES.

lines: A DEER WITH A COAT OF GOLD.
LAKSHMANA: NO DEER LOOKS LIKE THAT.
cards: The Ramayana. In the forest, Sita sees a deer with a coat of gold, flecked like jewels, and she wants it. Rama goes after it.
Lakshmana, his brother, warns them: no real deer looks like that. It's the demon Maricha in disguise, sent by Ravana. He's right.
Rama's arrow finds the deer, and as it dies, Maricha cries out in Rama's own voice: Ah, Sita! Ah, Lakshmana!

teach.h: A FALSE CRY. A MIND SURE OF IT.
teach.b: Sita hears the cry and is sure Rama is dying. She sends Lakshmana after him, and with both brothers gone, Ravana comes. One of the great turns of the Ramayana begins with a mind taking something false for real.
Read it with Patanjali's list in hand. Sutras 1.5 to 1.11 say every turning of the mind is one of five kinds, and each can bring pain or not.
One: pramana, right knowledge, by perception, inference or reliable testimony. Lakshmana had it: no real deer looks like that. Two: viparyaya, error, a picture that doesn't match the real form.

A demon seen as a deer. The classic Indian example is a coiled rope at dusk taken for a snake. Three: vikalpa, knowing that follows words with nothing real behind them; Indian logicians liked the example of a hare's horn.
Four: nidra, sleep. Patanjali counts even dreamless sleep as a turning; the commentator Vyasa notes that you wake and say, I slept well. Five: smriti, memory, holding on to what you've lived.
And here's the twist: right knowledge is on the list. Yoga is the stilling of all five, the true ones too, because even a true thought is the mind moving. Why sort them?
Many teachers say a turning you can name loosens its grip.
It's a map Hindu meditators have used for centuries: notice the turning, name it, and don't run after it.
In the Ramayana, chasing one golden deer cost almost everything. In a sit, naming the turning is how you stop chasing.

how: Students of the Yoga Sutras learn the five vrittis as a map for meditation, labeling movements of the mind so they can be noticed and released rather than followed.

games.q: it's dusk. you see a coiled shape on the path and jump back: a snake! then you look again: a rope. which turning was the snake?
games.why: viparyaya: a wrong knowing, a picture that doesn't match the real form. the rope and snake is the classic Indian example.

practice: Be a gentle sorter: when a thought arises, give it one of five silent labels.
Knowing, a car outside; error, that voice was the fridge; imagining, a conversation that isn't happening; sleep, a drifting fog; memory, something from yesterday.
Don't argue with any of them; label, let it pass, and come back to the breath.

wordCard.voice: Vritti, a turning, a whirl of the mind. Patanjali names five kinds: right knowledge, error, imagination, sleep and memory, the movements yoga learns to still.

orig.note: Sanskrit vṛtti: a turning, a whirl, a movement of the mind. Patanjali names five kinds.
